:::{#def-moore-penrose}
#### Moore-Penrose inverse

A **Moore-Penrose inverse** of an $m \times n$ matrix $\matr{A}$
is an $n \times m$ matrix $\matr{G}$ satisfying all four conditions

1. $\matr{A} \matr{G} \matr{A} = \matr{A}$;
2. $\matr{G} \matr{A} \matr{G} = \matr{G}$;
3. $\tp{(\matr{A} \matr{G})} = \matr{A} \matr{G}$;
4. $\tp{(\matr{G} \matr{A})} = \matr{G} \matr{A}$.

Condition 1 says $\matr{G}$ is a generalized inverse (@def-generalized-inverse).

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-moore-penrose}
#### Checking the four conditions

For $\matr{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$,
the matrix $\matr{G} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$ satisfies all four:
$\matr{A} \matr{G} = \matr{G} \matr{A} = \matr{A}$ and $\matr{A}^2 = \matr{A}$,
so conditions 1 and 2 read $\matr{A} = \matr{A}$,
and conditions 3 and 4 hold because $\matr{A}$ is symmetric.

The generalized inverse $\matr{G}' = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$ of $\matr{A}$
(@exm-generalized-inverse) is not a Moore-Penrose inverse:
$\matr{A} \matr{G}' = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$,
which is not symmetric, so condition 3 fails.

:::
